documentation.title: Loaded sliding on a curved monotone surface
documentation.description:
The first model in the suite that BOTH carries load across the contact interface AND slides along a surface whose normal turns while it does so. Everything else with slidingType="large" is one or the other, and a flat interface is exactly where small-sliding kinematics are already exact, so no loaded testcase before this one could tell a right geometric tangent from a missing one.
The primary body's top edge is the parabola h(x) = 1 + 0.05*x^2 cut into three LINE3 faces. A LINE3 interpolates a quadratic exactly, so each face reproduces the parabola and the normal turns CONTINUOUSLY across face boundaries -- deliberately, since a faceted surface would mix curvature under load with a discontinuous normal and a failure would not say which caused it. The secondary block is non-matching by construction, its bottom edge lies ON the parabola so the initial gap is zero, and its top is FLAT so the load resultant is exactly p*L. Only u_x is prescribed there, leaving the block free to rise, settle and tilt: sliding a conforming block along a parabola opens a wedge linear in x that a rigid rotation closes exactly.
WHAT IT ASSERTS
1. contactForceY = 6e6 = 1e7 * 0.6, the vertical equilibrium of the secondary body. It holds for ANY pressure distribution, segmentation and curvature. It is reported per component because the scalar totalContactForce = INT p dG cannot serve: on a curved patch it overcounts by 1/cos(theta) per point. contactForceX is NOT independent -- it is whatever the u_x reaction balances. 2. numCells 6 -> 5, numPoints 12 -> 10, numContactElements 6 -> 5, as the block slides strictly inside one primary face and the cut in its second element disappears. Frozen under slidingType="small". Integers, so they cannot drift. 3. integratedArea, which must NOT move: a partition is a partition of the same surface however it is cut.
WHY THE LOAD IS LARGE. A parabola has non-constant curvature, so a block meshed onto it and then slid is slightly too curved for the surface it now rests on. The rigid rotation closes the LINEAR part of that mismatch; nothing removes the quadratic part, because a geometrically LINEAR body cannot perform a finite rotation without spurious strain. What is left is a Hertzian contact whose patch grows as sqrt(load), and the load is chosen so the patch covers the interface and the active set is settled from the first iteration. That is why this testcase asserts an equilibrium resultant rather than a pressure distribution.
The geometric tangent is deliberately not built, so convergence is linear at a rate of about p/E rather than quadratic -- worth at most one iteration of four, and only for a model whose contact pressure is a sizeable fraction of its modulus, which a small-strain model cannot have. idbcHandling="elimination" because under "penalty" the inhomogeneous Dirichlet rows hold nodal reactions Newton cannot reduce, so residualErr stalls while the answer is bit-identical.
